newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition stages huge New Year rally.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition stages huge New Year rally.

text.p: At least a quarter of a million people staged a huge New Year rally in Belgrade to demand democracy in Serbia, blowing whistles and ringing alarm clocks in an ear-splitting rebuff to President Slobodan Milosevic.

The autocratic Socialist (SPS) leader only hours before had ignored six straight weeks of opposition street protests against electoral fraud in his New Year's message to federal Serbian-led Yugoslavia, saying 1996 had been a very good year.

Western sources said Milosevic and Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic also snubbed a group of European Union diplomats who tried on Tuesday, New Year's Eve, to hand-deliver a message urging democratic changes in Serbia.

They found a deputy foreign minister and came away with the impression that Serbian authorities were ready to respond to pressure for democratisation, given teeth by Western threats to withhold financial aid for Yugoslavia's ruined economy.

But Milosevic's calculated disregard of the opposition campaign mounted by the Zajedno (Together) coalition backed by university students poured cold water on hopes that the issue could be promptly resolved.

That did not dampen the spirit of Zajedno's faithful, however. They clogged Belgrade's central Republic Square and adjoining streets in a multitude that seemed to surpass peak protest turnouts of 200,000-plus earlier in December.

Despite a new ban on street marches after a riot involving Zajedno and government loyalists, police authorised the rally and kept their distance, judging that the normal festive mood of New Year would be politically harmless.

Zajedno's revellers blew whistles and set off fireworks and alarm clocks ringing at the stroke of midnight as if time were running out for effective one-party leftist rule in Yugoslavia dating to 1945.

The noise largely drowned out speeches and music from a makeshift stage. A Zajedno leader, Vuk Draskovic, was overheard roaring: "Happy New Year! Let us crown in 1997 what we started in 1996. Long live a new democratic Serbia!"
Six students shut themselves in a cage while a magician performed a trick with disappearing ballots in a box, lampooning the Socialists for their fraud.
About 20 students dodged Milosevic's security forces, managing to get within 10 metres (yards) of the president's home in the elite residential district of Dedinje, witnesses said.

Opposition activists planned to demonstrate again with drums, whistles, pots and pans from 7.30 to 8 p.m. (1830-1900 GMT) on Wednesday to symbolically override state television's prime-time newscast airing at that time.
Tens of thousands of Zajedno activists also rallied in the provincial towns of Kraljevo, Leskovac and Jagodina.
In his New Year message on state television and radio, Milosevic wished his people a happy New Year and pledged free market reforms in a possible sop to Western concerns.

Milosevic only obliquely alluded to the political crisis triggered by the SPS's annulment of municipal election results that awarded control of 15 of Serbia's 18 largest towns, including Belgrade, to the opposition.

"Even if one takes into account the foreign and domestic disturbances to which we have been subjected, especially in the last few months, it can be said that we have used this year very well," he said.
A report by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) recommends that Milosevic acknowledge the Zajedno victories and initiate broader democratic reforms.
